panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial lung-window CT shows arrowed well-circumscribed central round lesion in right middle lobe in case of pulmonary carcinoid tumor, matching central pulmonary nodule manifestation. B: Axial mediastinal-window contrast-enhanced CT shows same arrowed soft-tissue density central nodule in right middle lobe attributed to pulmonary carcinoid tumor. C: Coronal lung-window CT shows same arrowed well-circumscribed central lesion in right middle lobe in pulmonary carcinoid case. D: FDG-PET shows same arrowed central right lung lesion with mild hypermetabolism SUV 2.8 described in caption and in-text, corresponding to pulmonary carcinoid tumor nodule; FDG avidity not in vocabulary so recorded as proposed finding while anatomic nodule tagged from vocabulary.

(A, B) Axial views (lung and mediastinal windows); (C) Coronal view (lung window); (D) FDG-PET scan. in_text_mentions: In the evaluation of her dyspnea, a chest computed tomography (CT) angiography was performed, ruling out pulmonary embolism but detecting a homogeneous, well-circumscribed pulmonary nodule measuring 19 mm in the middle lobe (ML). On fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET), the lesion showed mild hypermetabolism with a standardized uptake value (SUV) of 2.8 (Fig. 1). A low-grade NET was suspected. Two transbronchial biopsies were inconclusive. Serum chromogranin A and 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels were elevated, indicating a functional NET.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: H&E of subcutaneous metastasis of pulmonary carcinoid; expanding nodule shows organoid solid neoplasia consistent with bronchial carcinoid. B: H&E solid area of subcutaneous metastasis of lung carcinoid showing organoid neuroendocrine growth. C: High-power H&E explicitly describes salt-and-pepper chromatin, textbook neuroendocrine cytology of carcinoid metastasis. D: TTF-1 IHC of same subcutaneous metastasis of lung carcinoid; IHC shows retained organoid nesting visually, TTF-1 positivity supports lung origin but not in vocabulary so proposed. E: Chromogranin-A IHC strong diffuse positivity with cordonal/trabecular pattern in subcutaneous metastasis of pulmonary carcinoid. F: Synaptophysin IHC strong diffuse positivity in same subcutaneous metastasis of lung carcinoid with retained organoid architecture.

in_text_mentions: , speckled chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. The immunohistochemical study revealed positivity of the neoplastic cells with antibodies for Cam5.2, chromogranin, sinaptophysin, CD56, and TTF-1 (thyroid transcription factor 1). No staining was obtained with other markers (Ck7, Ck20, and Napsin-A). The tumor had no mitosis or necrosis and the KI67 index was 2%. The morphological features, together with the immunohistochemical profile (namely TTF-1 positivity) of the tumor, in the patient clinical context, were consistent with subcutaneous metastasis of a carcinoid tumor of the lung (Fig. 3).

caption: 'relatively uniform, hyperchromatic nuclei with finely granular ("salt-and-pepper") chromatin, a characteristic feature indicative of neuroendocrine differentiation'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: High-power H&E of bronchoscopic biopsy from a human patient; caption explicitly attributes the findings to a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor 'most consistent with a typical bronchial carcinoid,' showing the textbook nested/trabecular neuroendocrine architecture and salt-and-pepper chromatin without pleomorphism, necrosis, or elevated mitoses. Article title 'Young and Non-Smoking: An Unusual Case of Bronchial Carcinoid' supports a young adult patient. [raw subtype: typical] B: Low-power H&E overview of the bronchoscopic biopsy fragments showing bronchial mucosa infiltrated by the neoplastic proliferation; real human-patient histopathology of bronchial carcinoid with the nested neuroendocrine growth pattern described in the caption, though fine chromatin detail is not resolvable at this magnification. [raw subtype: typical] C: Medium-power H&E of the bronchoscopic biopsy showing the monotonous tumor population in nests/trabeculae...
panels.attribution_text: Constantin et al. Young and Non-Smoking: An Unusual Case of Bronchial Carcinoid.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2026. doi:10.3390/diagnostics16142190. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Microscopic examination of the bronchoscopic biopsy specimens revealed multiple fragments of bronchial mucosa infiltrated by a neoplastic proliferation composed of cells arranged predominantly in nests and trabecular patterns. The tumor cells were round to polygonal in shape, displaying relatively uniform, hyperchromatic nuclei with finely granular (“salt-and-pepper”) chromatin, a characteristic feature indicative of neuroendocrine differentiation. Furthermore, the cytoplasm was moderate in amount and poorly defined, contributing to the overall monotonous appearance of the tumor population. Importantly, no significant nuclear pleomorphism, necrosis, or increased mitotic activity was identified in the examined sections, findings that argue against a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma. In addition, the preserved architectural organization and lack of aggressive histological features further support the diagnosis of a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, most consistent with a typical bronchial carcinoid. These histopathological findings are in accordance with established diagnostic criteria, according to which typical carcinoids are defined by fewer than 2 mitoses per 2 mm2 and absence of necrosis, whereas atypical carcinoids demonstrate higher mitotic activity and/or focal necrosis. Furthermore, typical carcinoids are characterized by a relatively low metastatic potential, with reported rates of lymph node involvement and distant metastasis remaining limited [5]. In addition, more recent classifications have incorporated supplementary phenotypic, molecular, and genetic features into the diagnostic framework of these tumors [6]. Moreover, complementary microbiological and cytological analyses of bronchial aspirates were negative, thereby excluding infectious processes as well as alternative malignant etiologies, and reinforcing the specificity of the histopathological diagnosis.

B: Panel B is IHC for chromogranin A in same liver metastasis, directly captioned as positive in neoplastic cells. C: Panel C is IHC for synaptophysin in same liver metastasis, directly captioned as positive in neoplastic cells. D: Panel D is TTF-1 IHC of same liver metastasis captioned as expressed by neoplastic cells, supporting lung origin of atypical bronchial carcinoid; architecture visible, TTF-1 not in vocabulary so in proposed_findings.

panels.figure_caption: Photomicrograph showing the presence of an epithelial proliferation made of sheets of moderately atypical cells. (HE, 200X) (A). An immunohistochemistry study revealed the expression of chromogranin A (B), synaptophysin (C), and TTF-1 (D) by the neoplastic cells.
in_text_mentions: The pathological evaluation indicated liver parenchyma infiltrated by an organoid epithelial growth composed of thin sheets and cords of tumor cells. Proliferating cells sometimes showed nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin and some mitotic figures (6 mitoses per 10 high power fields (HFP)). On the neoplastic cells, immunohistochemistry showed the presence of chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) (Figure 4). Therefore, the diagnosis of atypical bronchial carcinoid of the upper right lung lobe, metastatic to the liver and bones was established.

panels.rationale: Real human patient thoracic CT (mediastinal window) showing a 3x3x2cm spiculated nodule in the right upper lung lobe, marked with a red arrow. The article title 'Atypical Bronchial Carcinoid Tumor Revealed by Liver Biopsy' provides disease attribution. The nodule represents the primary tumor manifestation of the atypical bronchial carcinoid. The spiculated morphology and peripheral location are atypical for bronchial carcinoid (which usually presents as a well-circumscribed central/hilar mass), consistent with the 'atypical' designation in the article title. [raw subtype: atypical]

in_text_mentions: year-old lady presented with persistently poor control of her asthma symptoms. She had a long-standing history of difficult asthma, frequently requiring oral prednisolone therapy.
